author: Autodesk
description: This graph generates the transform data for the FK to IK Machine Learning Example
documentation:
## Generate Data

### What it does
This graph generates a dataset that can be used to train a neural network that acts as an inverse kinematic solver for a 3-axis mechanical rig.

### Inputs and outputs 

The main input to the graph is an array of transforms, `pivot_locators`, that represent the pivot points of each axis in the rig's rest pose. These transforms can be modified by moving the associated `locator*` in the Maya scene. You can set the number of random samples, as well as a randomization seed on the `num_samples` and `seed` ports of the `data_generator` compound. 

You can optionally input an array of `meshes` to represent the rig geometry. 

The output of the graph are two NumPy array files, saved as `.npy`, that contain the paired input and output data, also known as features, for each sample to be used during the network training process. 

To save the generated data as `.npy` files for training outside of the graph, set the desired path and file name on the `input_features_path` and `output_features_path` of the `write_data_to_disk` compound, and then set the `write_data` port to checked. 

### Useful information

This example is intended to be paired with the `neural_network` example graph to show an end-to-end machine learning pipeline where data is procedurally generated, a neural network is trained on that data, and then the trained neural network is deployed to accomplish the intended task. 

In this case, we are approximating an inverse kinematic (IK) solver on a 3-axis mechanical rig. Each axis consists of a revolute joint that rotates about a single axis. 
We can leverage the fact that the forward kinematic (FK) solver is much easier to set up than an analytic or numerical IK solver, which can be seen in the `XZZ_FK` compound.

The `data_generator` compound generates three random angles, one for each axis of rotation for our rig, computes the FK solve using the `XZZ_FK` compound, and then measures the resultant end effector location. These are then assembled into arrays of samples to be used with the accompanying training script using PyTorch in your python IDE of choice.

During the training process, then network uses the paired inputs `[x, y, z]` and outputs `[theta_1, theta_2, theta_3]` to learn the patterns in the dataset, such that we can input a new end effector position `[x, y, z]` to our trained network, and it will predict the joint rotation values `[theta_1, theta_2, theta_3]` required for the rig to reach that position, effectively performing an IK solve.
